Subject: Private runtime — outbound IP / firewall expectations

Hi Stephanie / team,

Thanks again for the demo yesterday. Our infra/security leads asked for a concise list of what Ceres needs to allow from our perimeter for a private (VPC) deployment of Redwood's runtime. A few specific asks from our side: 
- Can you provide the minimum outbound IPs (or CIDRs) that must be whitelisted for the control plane and pull/update channels?
- Are FQDN-based allowlists acceptable (we prefer FQDNs to avoid static IP allocations)?
- What ports/protocols and TLS/SNI behavior should we expect?
- Any special requirements for telemetry/metrics (where do build agent and runtime send telemetry?)

We also need a simple acceptance checklist for our firewall team and a CSV/manifest we can drop into our change request. Attaching our initial network diagram in case it helps (we'll follow up with the architecture PDF).

Goal: get a baseline list we can use to open the change ticket this week.

Thanks,
Danielle

Hi Danielle — thanks for the clear list. Below is a concise, operational summary to use with your firewall/change team. I'm including a small CSV template (attached) you can drop into your ticket. If you want, we can run through the checklist on a quick call — suggest 30 minutes next week.

High‑level expectations (private runtime / VPC):
1) Control plane & update channels
   - For control plane callbacks and model updates Redwood requires a small set of stable egress IPs for reachability when customers opt into Redwood's managed control plane. Typical expectation: customer NATs outbound traffic to a static set of IPs the customer owns, or allowlisted IPs we provide if you prefer host‑level pinning.
   - If you cannot provide static outbound IPs, FQDN‑based allowlisting is acceptable only when used with TLS+SNI enforcement AND your proxy preserves SNI. Note: FQDN-only may make troubleshooting longer (DNS caching, CDNs).

2) Ports & protocols
   - HTTPS (443) required for all control plane and artifact pulls.
   - TLS 1.2+ recommended; TLS 1.3 preferred.
   - mTLS is supported for high‑assurance customers; we can provide certs for mutual auth if you'd like to enable mutual TLS for control plane endpoints.

3) Outbound behavior and NATing
   - Preferred: customer provides static NAT egress (single IP or a small CIDR) that we can reference in our allowlist manifest.
   - Alternative: proxy with SNI/Host passthrough — allowlist FQDNs: control.redwood-inference.com, updates.redwood-inference.com, telemetry.redwood-inference.com.

4) Telemetry & metrics
   - Minimal telemetry: runtime sends anonymized usage and health pings to telemetry.redwood-inference.com (443).
   - If you require telemetry to remain on‑prem, we offer an opt‑out and a push model for metrics ingestion (requires additional configuration).

5) Egress filtering / outbound ACLs
   - Allow outbound 443 to the control FQDNs or to the static IPs in the attached registry.
   - Block non‑standard outbound ports from the runtime hosts; only necessary outbound is 443.

Next steps / artifacts attached:
- exit-ip-registry-template.csv (small template with columns: purpose, ip_or_fqdn, port, note)
- Suggested acceptance criteria (short checklist embedded in the CSV).

If you prefer, we can also produce a signed attestation for your audit team once the allowlist is applied and validated.

Thanks — cc'ing Jonas for the firewall snippets and exact CIDR samples (Jonas, can you add the snippet below?)

—Stephanie

Thanks Stephanie / Jonas — this is very helpful. A couple quick clarifications from our security team: 
1) We prefer FQDN allowlisting because our NATs are shared across teams and we cannot guarantee static egress IPs for the first phase of the rollout. We'll need a written acceptance criteria checklist that says: when FQDN + SNI + TLS is used, Redwood will still provide troubleshooting support and a timeline for any escalations.
2) For telemetry: we will opt to keep metrics on‑prem for now. Please send the configuration steps to switch to the push model you mentioned.

I've attached our proxy architecture diagram and will open the change ticket this week with the three FQDNs you listed. Can you also confirm whether we should whitelist a specific A record range to speed up DNS failover scenarios (or is relying on the FQDN enough)?

Attachment: ceres-proxy-architecture.pdf (pdf)

If you can send the acceptance checklist and the push‑mode telemetry steps (bullet list), we can mark this as ready for our firewall change window next Wednesday.

Appreciate the quick turnaround.

—Danielle
Head of Cloud Ops, Ceres Health
